lead: Both engines burn fuel inside the cylinder, but ignite it differently. An SI (spark ignition) engine mixes petrol with air first, compresses the mixture, and lights it with a spark plug. A CI (compression ignition) engine compresses air alone until hot, then sprays diesel into it, and the fuel self-ignites. The four strokes stay the same. This difference sets compression ratio, load control, exhaust and typical use: petrol for scooters and small cars, diesel for trucks, tractors and generators.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.2 for bore, stroke, TDC, BDC and clearance volume, and Chapter 1.3 for the four-stroke sequence.

sections.h3: SI engine: the charge is mixed before it is compressed

blocks.text: SI means spark ignition. Petrol is the usual fuel. Air and fuel meet before the spark: in a carburettor, in the intake port by an injector, or early in the intake stroke. The cylinder therefore holds a premixed charge — fuel vapour spread through air — when compression starts. Hardware is in Unit 2.

Intake draws mixture; a throttle plate sets how much. Compression raises pressure and temperature. Near the end of compression the spark plug fires. A flame front starts at the plug and crosses the unburnt charge. Burning gas raises pressure, drives the piston down on the power stroke, and the exhaust stroke pushes gas out.

The flame takes milliseconds to cross the chamber, so spark is set slightly before top dead centre (TDC). This is spark timing. Too late and the burn finishes after the piston has dropped, wasting work.

Compression ratio is about 8:1 to 12:1. A higher ratio heats the end gas more. If it reaches autoignition temperature before the flame arrives, it burns suddenly and the engine knocks. The ratio is held below this knock limit (Unit 3).

Load is set by the throttle — the quantity of mixture admitted. At part load the plate is nearly closed and the piston works against a vacuum, wasting work as pumping loss. That is why a petrol car is thirsty in slow city traffic.

blocks.where: r is the compression ratio, a pure number; V<sub>s</sub> is the swept volume in cm³ or m³; V<sub>c</sub> is the clearance volume in the same unit.

sections.h3: CI engine: air is compressed, fuel is injected at the end

blocks.text: CI means compression ignition. There is no spark plug. Intake draws air only. Compression ratio is 16:1 to 22:1, about double SI. Compressing air heats it: starting near 300 K, a ratio of 18 gives roughly 900 to 950 K at the end of compression. Diesel self-ignites at about 250 °C, so this air is hot enough.

Near the end of compression the injector sprays diesel as a fine mist. Droplets evaporate and mix with air. After a short ignition delay the mixture autoignites at several points, and the rest burns as fast as it mixes. The injector delivers fuel; the spark plug delivers a spark. They are not interchangeable.

A CI engine has no throttle. Air flow stays almost the same at every load. Power is set by how much fuel is injected, so mixture strength changes. This is quality control against the SI engine's quantity control, and it avoids part-load pumping loss. That is why a diesel suits a bus or truck that stops and starts all day.

The high ratio raises ideal-cycle efficiency (Chapter 1.7), so a diesel usually beats a petrol engine of similar size on thermal efficiency. The price is high peak cylinder pressure, which needs heavier parts, plus nitrogen oxides (NOx) and smoke as the hard emissions (Unit 6). The fuels want opposite properties: diesel needs a high cetane number, meaning it ignites easily; petrol needs a high octane number, meaning it resists autoignition.

sections.h3: The two paths side by side

blocks.text: Exhaust differs too. An SI engine runs close to stoichiometric, so a three-way catalyst can clean carbon monoxide (CO), unburnt hydrocarbons and NOx together. A CI engine always runs lean, so CO and hydrocarbon levels are low but NOx and particulates are high, and a simple three-way catalyst does not work. That fact drives most diesel emission work.

sections.h3: Timing: spark and injection as events

blocks.text: Both timings are measured in crank angle degrees relative to TDC. Spark timing is where the plug fires, commonly 10° to 30° before TDC depending on speed and load. Injection timing is when the nozzle opens, commonly about 5° to 20° before TDC in a direct-injection diesel, and how long it stays open sets fuel quantity.

Spark too early gives high peak pressure and knock; too late gives low power and a hot exhaust. Injection too early lengthens ignition delay, so more fuel is ready when it finally burns and the engine runs rough with diesel knock; too late leaves unburnt fuel as smoke and wastes power. The maps and mechanisms belong to Unit 2.

figure.caption: Two parallel paths through the same four strokes. Notice that only the SI path carries fuel into the cylinder before compression, while the CI path makes the air hot first and injects fuel into it.

spec.aria: Two parallel block paths show SI ignition of a premixed charge by spark and CI injection into hot air for autoignition.

examples.question: An SI engine has a compression ratio of 9 and a CI engine has a compression ratio of 18. Both have a clearance volume of 50 cm³. Find the swept volume and the total cylinder volume of each engine.
steps: Write the definition: r = (V<sub>s</sub> + V<sub>c</sub>) ÷ V<sub>c</sub> = 1 + V<sub>s</sub>/V<sub>c</sub>, so V<sub>s</sub> = (r − 1) × V<sub>c</sub>.
Total cylinder volume at BDC is V<sub>s</sub> + V<sub>c</sub>. SI: 400 + 50 = 450 cm³.
examples.answer: The SI engine has a swept volume of 400 cm³ and a total cylinder volume of 450 cm³; the CI engine has a swept volume of 850 cm³ and a total cylinder volume of 900 cm³.
examples.check:
r_si = 9.0
r_ci = 18.0
Vc = 50.0
Vs_si = (r_si - 1) * Vc
Vs_ci = (r_ci - 1) * Vc
print(Vs_si)
print(Vs_ci)
print(Vs_si + Vc)
print(Vs_ci + Vc)

examples.question: A four-cylinder CI engine has a bore of 10 cm, a stroke of 12 cm and a compression ratio of 19. Find the clearance volume of one cylinder in cm³. The number of cylinders does not enter this calculation, because bore, stroke and compression ratio are all per cylinder.
steps: Swept volume of one cylinder: V<sub>s</sub> = (π/4) × d² × L, with d = 10 cm and L = 12 cm.
examples.answer: The clearance volume of one cylinder is about 52.4 cm³.
examples.check:
import math
d = 10.0
L = 12.0
r = 19.0
Vs = math.pi / 4 * d**2 * L
print(round(Vs, 1))
print(round(Vs / (r - 1), 1))

traps: A CI engine compresses air only. Writing that it compresses a fuel-air mixture is the commonest error.
Spark plug and injector are not interchangeable. One starts a flame in a ready mixture; the other creates the mixture by spraying fuel.
A diesel has no spark, but it does ignite. The fuel self-ignites in hot air.
Higher compression ratio is not automatically better. In SI it raises knock risk; in CI it raises peak pressure and NOx.
Keep load control straight: throttle controls air in SI (quantity control), injected fuel controls load in CI (quality control).

quiz.q: In which engine does fuel enter the cylinder before the compression stroke begins?
quiz.a: The SI engine. Fuel is mixed with air in the carburettor or intake port, so a premixed charge is compressed.

quiz.q: State the typical compression ratio ranges for SI and CI engines.
quiz.a: SI: about 8:1 to 12:1. CI: about 16:1 to 22:1.

quiz.q: Why does a CI engine not need a throttle plate to control load?
quiz.a: Air flow stays nearly full at all loads. Power is set by the quantity of fuel injected, so mixture strength changes instead of mixture quantity. No throttle means no pumping loss at part load.

quiz.q: Why is the compression ratio of an SI engine held below about 12:1?
quiz.a: The charge is premixed. A higher ratio heats the end gas, which may autoignite before the flame front reaches it, causing knock. Peak pressure also rises.

quiz.q: An engine has a swept volume of 900 cm³ and a compression ratio of 19. Find its clearance volume.
An engine has a clearance volume of 40 cm³ and a swept volume of 600 cm³. Find the compression ratio and say which type it likely is.
quiz.a: r = 1 + V<sub>s</sub>/V<sub>c</sub> = 1 + 600/40 = 1 + 15 = 16. A ratio of 16 points to a CI engine.

quiz.q: A mechanic claims he can run a petrol engine as a diesel by replacing the spark plug with an injector. Give two reasons why this fails.
quiz.a: First, the petrol engine's compression ratio of about 9 heats the air to only around 700 K (about 430 °C) at the end of compression, against roughly 950 K in a diesel. With heat loss to the walls the air is too cool, and stays cool for too short a time, for the diesel spray to autoignite reliably, so the fuel wets the walls and smokes instead of burning. Second, the diesel needs a much higher peak pressure, a high-pressure injection pump and a matching combustion chamber, which the petrol engine does not have; the throttle would also starve it of air.

quiz.q: A diesel bus and a petrol car work in the same stop-start city traffic. Explain which engine suffers more from part-load pumping loss and why.
quiz.a: The petrol car. Its throttle closes at part load, so the piston pumps against a vacuum and loses work every cycle. The diesel is unthrottled and sets load by fuel quantity, so its pumping loss stays small.

beyond: Not for the exam. Petrol engines now often inject fuel directly into the cylinder at high pressure, so the old hardware line between petrol and diesel has narrowed, but the spark still decides ignition. Low-temperature modes such as HCCI try to autoignite a premixed charge with no spark at all (see Unit 6, Advanced combustion). Diesel common rail systems push injection pressure into the 1000 to 2000 bar range so fuel and air mix faster. Search for gasoline compression ignition, spark-assisted HCCI and injection rate shaping.
